en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-śyāmaka-putra-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
Recorded by Master An as missing its translator, now appended to the Western Jin catalog.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vairañjī, together with twelve hundred and fifty [monks].
Bhikṣus, as well as bodhisattvas, kings, ministers, commoners, elders, householders, and laymen and laywomen beyond measure, all gathered together at one time.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Listen all with minds settled in tranquil concentration. When I first sought to attain the path of a bodhisattva in a previous life, my observance of the precepts was universally complete; with single-minded diligence, I cultivated and accumulated wisdom and practiced skillful means. My accumulated merits are beyond description."
"Neither the various devas, Śakra, Brahmā, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, kings, nor the common people are able to practice it.
When Ānanda heard the Buddha’s words, he adjusted his robes once more, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to hear it."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a bodhisattva named Sarvavyūha (All-Wondrous). He was benevolent and practiced giving, rescuing and aiding all living beings. He constantly cultivated the four immeasurable minds, delivering the world from peril and distress, and compassionately nurturing those in suffering."

At that time, while instructing the devas in the Tuṣita Heaven, he constantly fixed his mind during three periods of both day and night to contemplate the three realms—illuminating and observing the paths of good and evil among the people throughout the ten directions. He knew those who were filial and obedient to their parents, who honored and revered the Triple Gem, who were respectful and compliant toward their teachers and elders, and who cultivated various meritorious virtues; he constantly used his divine eye to survey the five destinies everywhere.

At that time, there was an elder in the kingdom of Kāśī who was solitary and without sons; both his eyes were blind. He harbored a heart’s wish to enter the mountains to seek unsurpassed wisdom, cultivate pure resolve, and take delight in the seclusion of empty and quiet places.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"This person has set his mind upon the study of the subtle and profound; yet, as he is blind in both eyes, if he enters the mountains, he may fall into ravines or pits, or encounter venomous insects, and thus suffer wrongful harm."
"If my life comes to an end, I shall become their son, provide for my parents, and remain until the end of their years.
Thereupon, when the Bodhisattva’s lifespan was exhausted, he descended to be born as a son in the home of blind parents.
His parents were filled with joy and held him in profound affection.
Originally, he had resolved upon a great aspiration to enter the mountains, but because a son was born to him, he remained and took delight in the world.
When the son was seven years old, he was named Śyāma.

Śyāma was profoundly filial, compassionate, and benevolent; he practiced the ten wholesome deeds—refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, deceit, drinking alcohol, false speech, frivolous talk, envy, cursing, and maintaining faith without doubt—advancing with diligence day and night.
He serves his parents as one serves Heaven; his speech is always accompanied by a smile and never offends another's feelings; his conduct accords with the Dharma and is never frivolous or deviant.
His parents are filled with joy, and their sorrows and anxieties cease.
When Śāṇa was over ten years old, he knelt upright and said to his parents:
"I have originally resolved upon the Great Mind and wish to enter the deep mountains to seek the aspiration for emptiness, stillness, and unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment."
How could one abandon one's fundamental vow for the sake of a son?
Human life in this world is subject to a hundred changes through impermanence; life is not of stone or metal, and its end arrives without fixed date.
I wish for you to fulfill your original intention and, while there is still time, enter the mountains to dwell in purity.
"I shall follow you of my own accord along with my parents, providing for them according to their wishes without missing the proper seasons.
His parents replied to Śyāma, "Your filial piety is known to Heaven; as long as you do not violate your original vow, we shall enter the mountains together."
Śyāma then gave away all the possessions in his house to the poor and destitute throughout the kingdom, and immediately entered the mountains together with his parents.
When Śyāma reached the mountains, he used reeds to build a hut for his parents and prepared beds and mats for them; it was neither cold nor hot, always providing the perfect climate.

Just one year after he entered the mountains, all manner of fruits grew in abundance, and when eaten, they were fragrant and sweet. Springs gushed forth, the water clear and cool, and lotuses of five colors bloomed in the ponds with brilliant luster. Sandalwood trees and various fragrant woods flourished, becoming twice as lush as they had been before.

When the winds and rains come in their proper seasons, it is neither cold nor hot; the leaves of the trees join together to shield against the rain and dew, and by shading out the sunlight, it remains perpetually cool beneath them.
Flying birds gathered and alighted; these wondrous and diverse species all produced the sounds of music to entertain their blind parents.

Lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, wolves, and venomous beasts all turned toward one another with hearts of compassion, no longer harboring any intent to harm each other; they all fed upon grasses and fruits, free from any sense of fear.
Deer, elk, bears, brown bears, and various other species of beasts all came to stay near Śyāma; their voices harmonized with one another, producing sounds of entertainment.

Śyāma was so profoundly filial and compassionate that when he walked upon the earth, he constantly feared it might suffer pain. The celestial deities and mountain spirits all assumed human forms to comfort the three practitioners day and night.
The three practitioners of the Way focused their minds in meditative concentration and were no longer subject to sorrow or anxiety.

Śyāma constantly accompanied his parents to gather a hundred kinds of fruits and melons to feed them; there was always a surplus. When thirsty, they drank from mountain springs, never lacking for anything.
At that time, his parents were thirsty and wished to drink; Śyāma, wearing a deer-skin garment, took a pitcher and went to fetch water.
Deer and various birds also went there to drink, feeling no fear or apprehension toward one another.
At that time, the King of Kāśī entered the mountains to hunt. From afar, the king saw a deer by the water’s edge and drew his bow to shoot it.

By mistake, the arrow struck Śyama in the chest. Wounded by the poisoned shaft, Śyama’s entire body was in agony, and he cried out loudly, “Who has taken a single poisoned arrow and shot and killed three men of the Path?”
Upon hearing the sound of human voices, the king immediately dismounted his horse and went before Śyāma.
Śyāma said to the king:
"Elephants die for their tusks; rhinoceroses for their horns; peacocks for their plumage; and deer for their hide and flesh."
"Now I have no horns, no tusks, no fur, and my skin and flesh are not fit to be eaten; for what crime am I now dying?
The King asked Śyāma, "What kind of person are you?"
Clad in deerskin, he was no different from the birds and beasts.

Śyāma said, "I am a man from within the king's realm who has come into these mountains with my blind parents; for more than twenty years I have studied the Way, never having been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects, yet now I have been shot and killed by the King."

At that very moment, a violent gale arose within the mountain, blowing down and breaking the trees; hundreds of birds wailed in lamentation, and lions, bears, brown bears, and other beasts all let out great roars, shaking the entire mountain.
The sun lost its brilliance, the flowing springs ran dry, the various flowers withered and died, and the earth trembled with thunderous vibrations.
At that time, the blind parents started up in alarm and said to one another:
"Śyāma went to fetch water and has not returned for a long time; could it be that he has been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects?"
The birds and beasts wail and cry out with sounds unlike their usual ones;
winds arise from all four directions and the trees are broken and snapped—there must surely be a portentous calamity.
At that time, the king was struck with terror and reproached himself greatly, saying:
"What I have done is monstrous!
I was originally shooting at a deer; it was merely by a mistake of my arrow that he was struck."
To shoot and kill a practitioner of the Way is a most grievous sin.
Because you satiated your greed for a small piece of meat, you must now undergo its heavy retribution.
I shall now offer the treasures of the entire kingdom, the contents of the treasuries, the palaces, the court ladies, the villages, and the cities to save your life.
Then the king stepped forward and pulled at the arrow in Śāṇa’s chest with his hand, but it was so deeply embedded that it could not be extracted.
Birds and beasts gathered from all directions like clouds, their cries shaking the entire mountain.
The king became even more terrified, and all his three hundred and sixty joints trembled.
Śyāma said to the king, "This is not the fault of Your Majesty; it is brought about by my own past transgressions."
I do not begrudge my own body or life, but I only pity my blind parents; they are already advanced in years and their two eyes can see nothing.
Once I am gone, they too shall eventually pass away, left with no one to rely upon or look up to.
"For this reason, I am consumed by such bitter and cruel remorse.
At that moment, the devas, nāgas, spirits of the mountains, spirits of the waters, and spirits of the trees were all moved with solemn awe.
The king spoke again with great earnestness:
"I would rather enter the hells and suffer punishment for a hundred kalpas than allow Śāṇa’s life to be restored.
He knelt long upon his knees before Śāṇa and repented, saying:

"If your son passes away, I shall no longer return to the kingdom, but will instead remain in the mountains to provide for your parents just as I did when you were here; do not let this cause you any anxiety."
"May all the devas, nāgas, and spirits bear witness that I shall not fail this vow.
When Śyama heard these words of the king's oath, although he was struck by a poisoned arrow, his heart was joyful and his mind delighted; even in death he felt no resentment, saying:
"Entrust my blind parents to the King for their support; thus the practitioner’s transgressions in this life will be extinguished, and he shall obtain immeasurable merit."
The king said, "Tell me where my parents are; before my son dies, tell me so that I may know.
Śyāma immediately pointed them out and spoke:
"From this path it is not far; you shall naturally see a thatched hut where my parents reside.
Your Majesty, proceed slowly so as not to frighten my parents, and with skillful means, explain our intentions to them."
Please convey my thanks to my parents on my behalf: impermanence has now arrived, and I must depart for the next world.

I do not begrudge my own life, but I only think of my parents who are aged and both blind; once I am gone, they will have no one to rely upon, and it is for this reason that I am so deeply distressed and tormented by grief.
Death is one's own destined lot, brought about by the consequences of past transgressions; there is no one who can escape it.
Now I repent before my parents for all the various evils I have committed since incalculable kalpas ago, so that these sins may be extinguished and merit may arise.
May I and my parents meet one another in every lifetime and never be separated.

May my parents live out their full natural lifespan without any anxiety or affliction; may devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly follow, protect, and assist them; may all calamities and disasters be extinguished; and may all their desires be fulfilled according to their wishes, occurring spontaneously and without effort.
The king then took several attendants and went directly to his parents' home.
After the king had departed, Śyāma suddenly passed away.
Birds and beasts all wailed loudly, circling above Śyāma’s corpse and licking the blood from his body with their tongues.
Hearing these sounds, the blind parents became even more terrified and stood there, wandering about in fear.
As the king traveled swiftly, his movement stirred the grasses and trees, producing a solemn sound like human voices;
the parents cried out in alarm, "Who is this person?"
"This is not the conduct of my son.
The king said, "I am the King of Kāśī.
Having heard that a man of the Way was practicing the Path in the mountains, I have come to provide offerings to this man of the Way."
The parents said, "It is most auspicious that Your Majesty has come; we are honored that you have condescended to travel so far from your exalted station to this humble wilderness.
Is Your Majesty’s person in good health and peace?"
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, the officials, and the people all well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, and are the five grains abundant?
"Do the neighboring countries not harm one another?
The king replied to the practitioner,
"By the grace of the practitioner, all are at peace."
The king inquired after the blind parents, saying:

"You have come to dwell in the mountains; has your mind not been weary and your labor arduous? Among the trees, have there been no predatory birds or wild beasts to harm you, O practitioners of the Way?"
"In these mountains, with cold and heat following their seasons, are you at peace in this present life?
The blind parents replied,
"By the profound grace of Your Majesty, we have always been at peace."

"I have a filial son named Śyāma, who constantly gathers a hundred kinds of fruits and melons for me; the mountain springs are always abundant, and the winds and rains in the mountains are harmonious, so that we lack nothing."
"I have grass mats upon which you may sit and fruits and melons whereof you may eat.
Śāṇa has gone to fetch water and will soon return.
When the king heard these words from the blind parents, his heart was again deeply grieved, and shedding tears, he said:
"I am a wicked and lawless man who entered the mountains to hunt. Seeing a herd of deer by the water's edge, I drew my bow and shot at them.
My arrow mistakenly struck the son of a *śramaṇa*. Because Śyāma’s body was pierced by the poisoned arrow and he was in great pain, he came to speak with the two *śramaṇas*."
Upon hearing this, the parents threw themselves to the ground, collapsing like the fall of Mount Tai, causing the earth to tremble.
The King then stepped forward to support them; the parents looked toward heaven and wailed, lamenting:

"Our son, Śyāma, was the most filial in all the world; his benevolence and kindness were unsurpassed. When he walked upon the earth, he always feared it might suffer pain; what crime has he committed now that you, O King, have shot and killed him?"
"Just now, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing down the trees; the hundred birds wailed and cried out, making the entire mountain resound with their lamentation.

For over twenty years I have lived in this mountain, yet never before have such calamities or portents occurred. I suspect that my son went to fetch water and has not returned for a long time; there must surely be some cause for this."
All the deities were startled and moved with solemnity.
The mother wailed and cried out, unable to stop herself, whereupon the father said:
"Cease for now!"
"In human life, there is no one who does not die; impermanence is natural and cannot be averted.
He then asked the king, "Where did you shoot Śyāma? Is he dead now, or is he alive?"
The King related everything that Śyāma had said in his own words to his blind parents.
Upon hearing these words from the King, they were once again overcome with grief and despair:
"If we lose our son at once, we shall both surely die as well; we pray that Your Majesty lead us both to stand before Śyāma’s corpse."

The king then led his blind parents to the corpse; the father embraced both of its feet, while the mother took its head onto her lap. Each of them used one hand to feel for the arrow in its chest and cried out to heaven:

"O gods, nāgas, mountain deities, tree deities, and water deities! Our son was benevolent and profoundly filial, as all you deities know. How can you not show even a single moment of compassion for our son, this virtuous child?"
The mother then licked the wound on Śyāma’s chest with her tongue, saying:
"I pray that the poison may enter my mouth; I am already old and my eyes see nothing, so I shall take this body in exchange for my son's life."
"Śyāma lives and I die; in my death, there is no regret.
Thereupon, the blind parents said:

"If Śyāma possesses such supreme sincerity and supreme filial piety that it is known by Heaven and Earth, then this arrow must be pulled out, the poison must be removed, and Śyāma shall be restored to life."

Thereupon, the seat of Śakra, the King of the Second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, shook violently. With his divine eye, he saw the two practitioners of the Way embracing their child and wailing; the Fourth Tuṣita Heaven, the various celestial palaces, and the dragon palaces all trembled solemnly.

Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings immediately descended from the fourth heaven; in the time it takes a person to stretch out an arm, they arrived and stood before Śyāma, pouring divine medicine into his mouth.
When the medicine entered Śyama’s mouth, the arrow pulled itself out, and he was restored to life as before.
His parents were filled with wonder and joy; seeing that Śyama, who had already died, had come back to life, both his eyes opened.

Birds and beasts all produced sounds of joy; the winds ceased and the clouds dispersed, so that the sun shone with redoubled brilliance. Springs gushed forth, and the various flowers of five colors and the hues of the trees were twice as magnificent as usual.

At that time, the king was filled with great joy, unable to contain himself; he prostrated before Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and then returned his salutations to his parents and to his son, Śyāma, saying:

"I wish to offer the wealth of my kingdom to this Way-man. I shall personally remain here to provide for him, so that my offenses in this life may be extinguished and my long-standing enmity may be removed."
Śyāma replied to the king, saying:
"If you wish to repay my kindness, Your Majesty should return to your kingdom and comfort your people, causing them all to uphold the five precepts.
Do not hunt or shoot again, for by prematurely harming insects and beasts, your body will find no peace in this present life, and when your lifespan ends, you shall enter the hells."
When people dwell in this world, affection is but temporary; separation lasts long, and one cannot remain forever.
Your Majesty, having possessed merit in former lives, you have now become king; do not, on account of having attained such sovereignty, indulge yourself in self-indulgence.
At that time, the king deeply reproached himself, vowing from then on to follow Śyāma’s instructions and never again dare to neglect them.

The several hundred people who had accompanied the king on the hunt saw that Śyāma was already dead, yet a divine being descended carrying medicine; as soon as it entered his mouth, he was restored to life. His parents’ eyes opened, and they all leaped for joy, resolving to uphold the five precepts and never violate them for the rest of their lives.

After the king returned to his kingdom, he issued a proclamation throughout the land: "All those who are poor, as well as those whose parents are blind like Śyāma, shall be provided for; none shall be abandoned. Those who violate this decree shall be subject to severe punishment."

Thereupon, because Śyāma had been restored to life, the people of the kingdom instructed one another from high to low to reverently observe the five precepts and practice the ten wholesome deeds; consequently, upon death they ascended to heaven, and none entered the three evil realms.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Among those gathered here, the one who was Śyāma in his previous life is my own self;
the blind father at that time is none other than my present father, King Śuddhodana."
The blind mother at that time was none other than my current mother, Queen Māyā;
the King of the Kāśī country was Ānanda;
and the Śakra Devendra of that time was Maitreya.
That I have swiftly attained the decisive realization of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way is entirely due to the compassionate kindness of my parents who nurtured me;
that I passed from death to life and moved the gods, dragons, spirits, and ghosts is the result of a filial son’s devotion to the profound weight of parental恩情 (en-qin);
and that I have now become a Buddha and am delivering the people of the nation is all due to the virtue of filial piety.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You must explain this extensively to all people: when one has parents, one must not fail to be filial.

The Way must be studied; it is through this that the spirit is saved from suffering and one later attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). All of this is brought about by compassion, filiality, and the study of the Way."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, commoners, elders, and householders all increased their reverence; they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, paid their respects, and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Bodhisattva Śyāma’s Sons.
